title: 500 Snails Mailed to Tahiti to Help Save Their Species
summary:
What is small, slow, and travels by overnight mail? Give up? It is 500 Partula snails! These tiny tree-dwelling snails were recently packed up at the Detroit Zoo in Michigan and shipped to the St. Louis Zoo in Missouri. Soon they will fly to Tahiti, an island in the Pacific Ocean, and be released into the wild.

Why would anyone mail snails? Because these snails are in trouble. Partula snails are native to French Polynesia. Long ago, people brought a predator snail called the rosy wolf snail to the islands to eat another invasive snail. But the rosy wolf snail also ate the Partula snails. The Partula population crashed.

For decades, the Detroit Zoo has been breeding Partula snails and sending them back to Tahiti by the thousands. The 500 snails on this trip were all born at the zoo. Each one has a tiny orange dot of safe paint on its shell. The dot glows under UV light, so scientists can find them later. Each year gets a different color.

At the St. Louis Zoo, the snails are eating a special diet to get ready for the wild. Then they will be released. This is part of a big program that has brought back 11 species of Partula snails that were once extinct in the wild. More than 17,000 snails have been returned.

Mark Vassallo from the Detroit Zoo says success means a self-sustaining population — snails that keep having babies on their own. So far, things are looking good for these little travelers.
why_it_matters: When people move animals to new places, whole species can disappear, and this shows how careful work by zoos can help fix a problem that humans caused.

background_read: French Polynesia (a group of many small islands in the Pacific Ocean, including Tahiti) is far from any big continent, so its animals are easy to harm when new species arrive.

Zoos around the world often breed rare animals in safe places and then release their young back into the wild — a plan called reintroduction — with animals like golden lion tamarins and black-footed ferrets.
When people move animals to new places, the newcomers sometimes eat or out-compete the local animals; cane toads in Australia and zebra mussels in American lakes are famous examples.
Article_Structure: WHO: Partula snails bred at the Detroit Zoo, cared for at the St. Louis Zoo, and studied by Mark Vassallo of the Detroit Zoo.
WHAT: 500 zoo-born snails were mailed from one zoo to another and will soon fly to Tahiti to be released into the wild.
WHERE: From Michigan to Missouri to Tahiti in French Polynesia, an island group in the Pacific Ocean.
WHY: To bring back Partula species that the invasive rosy wolf snail had wiped out in the wild.

perspectives.description: They are hopeful, because thousands of snails have come back and some are already having babies on their own in the wild.
They remember the trouble started when people moved a snail to a new place, so they stay watchful about what gets released and where.
For these tiny animals, the trip means leaving a safe zoo home and facing hungry rosy wolf snails out in the wild.
